clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant dystrophy caused by BEST1 mutations encoding bestrophin-1, a calcium-activated chloride channel on the basolateral membrane of the retinal pigment epithelium.
The pathognomonic combination is an abnormal electro-oculogram (reduced light rise, giving a low Arden ratio) with a normal full-field electroretinogram.
The classic egg-yolk (vitelliform) macular lesion evolves through recognised stages: previtelliform, vitelliform, pseudohypopyon, vitelliruptive (scrambled-egg), atrophic and cicatricial.
Central vision is often preserved for years or decades despite a striking fundus appearance, and the condition is frequently bilateral.
Choroidal neovascularisation is the principal sight-threatening complication and can arise even in younger patients.
Fundus autofluorescence shows markedly hyperautofluorescent vitelliform material owing to lipofuscin-like accumulation.
Penetrance and expressivity are variable, so relatives with a normal fundus may still show an abnormal electro-oculogram, aiding cascade assessment.
Biallelic BEST1 mutations cause a distinct recessive bestrophinopathy with a different, often more severe phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: Best vitelliform macular dystrophy results from mutations in BEST1, which encodes bestrophin-1, a calcium-activated chloride channel located on the basolateral membrane of the retinal pigment epithelium. Loss of normal channel function disturbs transepithelial ion and fluid movement and the generation of the light-evoked standing potential, which is why the electro-oculogram light rise is characteristically reduced while the photoreceptor-driven electroretinogram remains normal. Impaired retinal pigment epithelial handling of shed photoreceptor outer segments leads to accumulation of lipofuscin-like material within and beneath the epithelium at the macula, producing the yellow vitelliform lesion. Over time this material breaks down and disperses, and progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium and overlying photoreceptors culminates in atrophy and, in some eyes, secondary choroidal neovascularisation and fibrosis with loss of central acuity.
additionalDifferentials: Adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy (a pattern dystrophy)
Age-related macular degeneration with vitelliform or drusenoid change
Basal laminar (cuticular) drusen with vitelliform detachment
Acquired vitelliform lesions secondary to other maculopathies
additionalInvestigations: Electro-oculogram demonstrating a reduced light-peak to dark-trough (Arden) ratio
Optical coherence tomography of the macula showing subretinal vitelliform material
Fluorescein angiography where choroidal neovascularisation is suspected
Microperimetry to map central retinal sensitivity
redFlags: Sudden reduction in vision, metamorphopsia or a new central scotoma suggesting choroidal neovascularisation
Rapidly enlarging subretinal haemorrhage or exudate at the macula
Progressive bilateral central atrophy threatening reading vision
New distortion on home Amsler-grid monitoring
reference.prognosis: The long-term outlook is generally favourable, with useful central vision often retained into later adulthood; significant visual loss usually reflects macular atrophy or choroidal neovascularisation, and legal blindness, though possible, is uncommon.
pitfalls: Misattributing the maculopathy to age-related macular degeneration in older patients and missing the underlying dystrophy.
Being falsely reassured by a normal electroretinogram; the electro-oculogram is the discriminating test.
Overlooking early choroidal neovascularisation as simply progression of the vitelliform lesion.
Assuming an unaffected fundus excludes carrier status without electrophysiology or genetic testing.
Confusing the condition with adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy, which has a distinct course and inheritance.
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course (standard reference)
management: Adopt observation with regular macular imaging, as there is no established treatment to alter the underlying BEST1-related dysfunction
Treat choroidal neovascularisation, the main threat to sight, with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, including in younger patients
Surveil both eyes with serial optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence given the typically bilateral course
Give Amsler-grid instructions for self-detection of new metamorphopsia prompting urgent assessment
Arrange low-vision support and occupational adjustment if atrophy or cicatricial change reduces acuity
Confirm the diagnosis with electro-oculography and BEST1 testing, and provide genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal dominant condition
